title: Curated neurodegeneration axis signals are sensitive to cell composition and analytic choices: an adversarial re-analysis of a transcriptomic scoring pipeline
authors: Ghosh, N.; Sinha, K.
abstract: Background: Curated gene-set ("axis") scores are widely used to summarise disease biology in postmortem brain transcriptomes. In bulk tissue such scores can also change with cell-type composition, with broad transcriptome shifts in diseased tissue, or with analysis choices made after the results were seen. We tested these explanations on our own published pipeline, NeuroFate, whose preprint reported an Alzheimer's disease (AD) "neuronal vulnerability" axis and a Parkinson's disease (PD) "divergent" synuclein-mitochondrial axis. Results: A code audit found that the AD discovery axis averaged Sst, Pvalb and Lamp5 interneuron cell-type proportions together with its gene-expression features; that 90 endpoint x axis tests were run before the endpoints were locked; that axes were defined from the cohorts later cited as discovery evidence; and that the PD-divergent label came from an axis-specific rule defined after the result. Their contribution to the AD association could not be quantified because the donor-level data were not archived. In GSE7621 (16 PD, 9 controls) the synuclein-mitochondrial association reproduced (exact p = 0.0011) but depended on the scoring method (exact p from 0.001 to 0.057; with per-gene standardisation no axis reached Benjamini-Hochberg significance), lay at the 2.4th percentile of 10,000 expression-matched random probe sets (two-sided p = 0.06), and was attenuated by 76% (95% interval 26% to >100%) after adjustment for a dopaminergic-marker expression proxy (PD coefficient -1.13 to -0.27 SD). A small laser-captured cohort (GSE20141; 10 PD, 8 controls) was inconclusive: no axis reached p < 0.05, and the synuclein-mitochondrial effect had the same sign. In 1,000 simulated cohorts, a naive test called a purely composition-driven gene set significant in 82% of cohorts, whereas the proposed battery classified it as composition-independent in 5% while recovering a planted within-cell effect in 98% (moderate effect) and 50% (weak effect) of cohorts. Conclusions: The original axis associations do not establish composition-independent disease programs; their interpretation is sensitive to feature construction, scoring and adjustment for cell composition. Curated axis scores in bulk brain tissue should be reported with competitive null distributions, composition adjustment, exact small-sample inference, and endpoints and scoring fixed before analysis. We provide code for these checks.

title: Building computational benchmarks: an Omnibenchmark reimplementation of a single-cell preprocessing pipeline evaluation
authors: Choudhury, A.; Kitak, T.; Carrillo, B.; Busch, P.; Emons, M.; Gunz, S.; Koderman, M.; Luo, S.; Mallona, I.; Meara, A.; Wissel, D.; Robinson, M. D.
abstract: Background: In the past few years, we have seen a veritable surge in single-cell (e.g., RNA-sequencing) techniques and datasets, enabling increasingly detailed characterization of cellular heterogeneity across tissues and conditions. This surge in single-cell techniques has been complemented by a large number of analysis frameworks and pipelines, and a large parameter space and researcher degrees of freedom to use them. Many neutral benchmarks have been presented for various computational tasks, but most make design decisions that render them incompatible with each other, e.g., through the use of different datasets, metrics, or parameter sets. Results: We showcase Omnibenchmark, a recently developed framework to build reproducible, extensible, and standardized method comparisons for an arms-length benchmark that evaluates five single-cell RNA sequencing pipelines, spanning filtering, normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, on three datasets. The framework facilitates the broad investigation of pipelines used in single-cell data analysis while highlighting how the process of building benchmarks can be streamlined and unified. This standardization enables benchmarks to be extended in several directions, including broader parameter sweeps, comparisons across software versions and architectures, isolation of pipeline steps, and integration of additional pipelines, datasets, and metrics. As an example, our harmonization of pipelines highlighted that tools implement the (clustering) resolution parameter differently. Conclusions: Omnibenchmark provides a reproducible, extensible, and standardized approach for benchmarking. By unifying the process of benchmark construction, it can facilitate more consistent method comparisons and provides a foundation for broader, more flexible, and more sustainable benchmarking efforts.

title: The insect brain is specified by a conserved transcriptional program distinct from the segmental CNS
authors: Cabanas, N.; Veloso, A.; Zinzen, R.; Bucher, G.
abstract: The brain is the central processing center that integrates information to guide animal behavior, while the posterior CNS performs less central functions. To what degree this functional distinction is reflected in divergence of the genetic regulation remains unexplored, as well as the hypothesis of a distinct evolutionary origin of brain and trunk CNS. In insects, neuroblast biology is similar across the CNS, but the presence of brain-specific neuroblast types and differences in the gene sets involved in their spatial and temporal specification indicate divergence. However, a comprehensive and unbiased comparison of the regulatory code of brain versus trunk neuroblasts has been lacking. Here, we reveal the transcription factors expressed in insect embryonic neuroblasts by a combined single-cell analysis from the fly Drosophila melanogaster and the beetle Tribolium castaneum, for which we established a Gal4 enhancer trap system to generate a line marking NBs with tGFP. From the combined dataset of nearly 70,000 neuroblasts, we identified around 23,000 brain neuroblasts, from which we identified cell populations and their transcriptional signatures. We found 188 brain-specific TFs, including seven spatially restricted transcription factors not previously associated with neuroblasts (Hmx, CG15696, CG32532, dmrt99B, fD59A, TfAP-2, and Fer1). In addition to the expected canonical Type II NBs, we found two related clusters with intriguing transcriptional divergence. The large number of brain-specific TFs supports a profound divergence between the insect brain and posterior CNS. Together with recent work in vertebrates, our data confirm an ancient divergence of the brain from the trunk.

title: Optimisation of single-nuclei isolation and RNA sequencing of parasitic nematodes
authors: Buddenborg, S. K.; Morrison, A.; Fletcher, A. C.; Kieninger, M. R.; Ng, B. L.; Maitland, K.; Hart, E.; Bartley, D.; Duque-Correa, M. A.; Doyle, S. R.
abstract: Single-cell/nuclei transcriptomics has revolutionised our understanding of cell, tissue, and organismal biology in humans and model organisms across health and disease. However, for non-model species, reassessment and refinement of conventional methods is needed to address novel technical and biological challenges. Here, we evaluate three established nuclei isolation protocols and, building on these experiences, develop an optimised protocol for single-nuclei isolation of parasitic nematodes (SNIP). SNIP recovered 1.7- to 4.1-fold more nuclei than the three established protocols, and 3.2-fold more RNA per nucleus than the best-performing of these. We validated SNIP across macroscopic and microscopic life stages and both sexes of two phylogenetically distinct gastrointestinal nematodes, Haemonchus contortus and Trichuris muris, and used it to generate single-nuclei RNA-seq data revealing sex- and stage-specific gene expression and putative tissue-specific expression in both species. By enabling flexibility with frozen samples and consistent recovery across diverse parasitic nematode life stages, SNIP provides a practical foundation for building cell and nuclei atlases in other non-model species, toward advancing understanding from fundamental biology to infection and disease.

title: Genetic control and tissue specificity of transcriptomic rhythmicity
authors: Chauquet, S.; Hivert, V.; Weger, B.; Gachon, F.; Yengo, L.; Shah, S.; McRae, A. F.
abstract: Circadian rhythms influence molecular traits in most tissues, yet genetic studies mostly treat molecular measurements as static. In particular, genetic effects on gene expression are typically investigated through expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) studies, which ignore sampling time and therefore miss genetic effects on rhythm parameters such as amplitude and acrophase. In this study, we used a cosinor-based joint genotype-by-rhythm interaction framework applied to GTEx version 10 gene expression data, with donor inferred phase as a proxy for circadian time. We first identified rhythmically expressed genes in 49 of the 50 tissues profiled in GTEx. We then tested common variants within 50 kb of each rhythmic gene's transcription start site for genetic regulation of transcriptomic rhythmicity. We identified 167 circadian expression QTLs (cd-eQTLs), comprising 54 lead signals for 51 genes across 28 tissues. Most cd-eQTLs altered oscillation amplitude, while others affected acrophase or both. We then investigated the tissue specificity of cd-eQTLs and found that those acting on core circadian genes had consistent effects across tissues, whereas those acting on clock-regulated genes were largely tissue-specific. A phenome-wide association study in the Pan-UK Biobank linked 34 cd-eQTLs to 100 phenotypes, including self-reported chronotype, adiposity, blood cell counts and blood biochemistry. These results show that genetic variation shapes circadian gene expression in a tissue-dependent manner, and that accounting for time of day reveals regulatory effects that static eQTL analyses cannot detect.

title: scTGCL: A Transformer-Based Graph Contrastive Learning Approach for Efficiently Clustering Single-Cell RNA-seq Data
authors: Khan, M. S. A.; Kabir, M. H.; Faisal, M. M.
abstract: Motivation: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables characterization of cellular heterogeneity at unprecedented resolution. However, accurate clustering of scRNA-seq data remains challenging due to high dimensionality, dropout-induced sparsity, and technical noise. Existing contrastive learning methods usually create augmented views by perturbing gene expression values, so the uncertainty in cell-cell relationships caused by dropout events is not properly modeled. Results: We propose scTGCL, a novel Transformer-based graph contrastive learning framework that learns robust and discriminative cell representations directly from gene expression data. scTGCL employs multi-head self-attention to adaptively construct weighted cell-cell graphs and a Transformer encoder to generate cell embeddings from them, capturing diverse biological relationships. For contrastive augmentation, we apply feature-level gene masking together with attention masking that randomly drops edges of the learned attention matrices, enabling the model to withstand dropout events and technical noise. A symmetric contrastive loss maximizes agreement between original and augmented representations, while joint optimization with reconstruction and imputation losses preserves biological interpretability. Extensive experiments on twenty real and simulated scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that scTGCL achieves the highest average performance among nine state-of-the-art baseline methods in clustering accuracy, normalized mutual information, and adjusted Rand index, while also achieving superior imputation performance and substantially lower runtime on large-scale datasets. Furthermore, biological analysis confirms that the learned clusters align with known cell types and yield biologically interpretable pathway enrichment, validating the utility of scTGCL for downstream cell annotation and marker gene discovery. Availability and Implementation: The source code and test data are freely available at GitHub (https://github.com/ShoaibAbdullahKhan/scTGCL)

title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
authors: van Haren, J. J. G.; de Lange, F. P.; Kotz, S. A.; De Martino, F.
abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Yet, how all these concurrent mechanisms unfold in time remains underexplored. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in participants listening to stochastic tone sequences with periodically shifting inferential statistics, we modelled the temporal, spatial, and spectral dynamics of stimulus-specific repetition suppression, surprisal, model updating, and prior precision. By concurrently tracking these computational parameters within this dynamic auditory environment, we revealed a distinct chronological hierarchy governing predictive and adaptive processing. Prior precision states - reflecting expectations - emerged earliest, followed by rapid and concurrent repetition suppression and surprisal - reflecting local acoustic attenuation and global mismatch detection. These initial dynamics culminated in subsequent, distributed model updates within fronto-parietal networks. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

title: Mathematical model for visual cortical development based on molecular mechanisms underlying the generation and elimination of dendritic spines
authors: Tanaka, S.; Miyashita, M.
abstract: In the developing brain, neural circuits are elaborated by the activity-dependent rewiring of synaptic connections. Our earlier self-organization model, which was built on the assumption that axon terminals compete with each other to form synaptic contacts to single dendritic spines, successfully reproduced spatiotemporal receptive fields and orientation-direction joint maps (Tanaka et al., 2020). It has been reported that most synaptic contacts are en passant types rather than axonal terminals (Turegano-Lopez et al., 2024). This finding contradicts our assumption that each axon terminal selects an appropriate dendritic spine. Recent microscopic observations have shown that dendritic spines are more motile than presynaptic boutons (Bonhoeffer and Yuste, 2002; Deng and Dunaevsky, 2005). In addition, the current view of synaptic rewiring in early development is that filopodia spontaneously generated along dendrites transform into spines by establishing contacts with neighboring axonal boutons to form synapses whereas spines of inappropriate synapses are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner (Deng and Dunaevsky, 2005). In this theoretical study, we mainly focus on the processes of spine generation, maturation, and elimination to rebuild a mathematical model of synaptic rewiring, incorporating recent experimental findings on actin polymerization and depolymerization (Ridley, 2006) under the activation of Rho-GTPases (Mackay and Hall, 1998) mediated by the binding of variant forms of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Binder and Scharfman, 2004; Lesmann and Brigadski, 2009; Kuczewski et al., 2009) to neurotrophin receptors such as tropomyosin kinase receptor B (TrkB) (Klein et al., 1989) and the low-affinity-nerve growth factor receptor (p75NTR) (Yamashita et al., 1999). TrkB receptors are dephosphorylated by chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) (de Vivo et al., 2013) mediated by protein-tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPsigma (Kurihara and Yamashita, 2012) in an age-dependent manner. The model describes the generation or elimination of dendritic spines of visual cortical neurons under actin polymerization and depolymerization to establish appropriate synaptic contacts on afferent fibers of cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus. The simulations based on the new model reproduced not only simple-cell-like receptive fields (DeAngelis et al., 1999) and orientation-direction maps (Shmuel and Grinvald, 1996) but also a characteristic profile of the total number of synapses, which shows an early increase and a delayed decrease during the critical period (Li et al., 2006; White and Fitzpatrick, 2007). It is also demonstrated that whereas orientation selectivity is elevated almost monotonically throughout the critical period, the formation of direction selectivity is delayed behind the formation of orientation selectivity, which is likely promoted by the pruning of inappropriate synapses (Grigonis et al., 1988; Bourgeois et al., 1993; Elston et al., 2009; Faust et al., 2021).

title: Acute social defeat induces cannabinoid type 1 receptor-dependent synaptic depression in the anterior ventral subiculum to anterior hypothalamic nucleus pathway to drive social avoidance in male mice
authors: Woo, C.; Lee, S.; Lee, C.; Yoon, D.; Choi, S.; Kang, S. J.; Choi, K.; Shin, K. S.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Social avoidance is a protective response that limits exposure to harmful social stimuli. Although avoidance is a characteristic stress phenotype, its circuit-level regulation remains unclear. The ventral subiculum (vSUB), a major hippocampal output, projects to the anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN), a key region for stress responses. METHODS: Male mice underwent acute social defeat stress (ASDS) or subthreshold social defeat stress. We combined social interaction, open field, and elevated plus maze testing with optogenetic-assisted slice recording, pharmacology, pathway-specific chemogenetics and optogenetics, retrograde and anterograde transsynaptic tracing, and in situ hybridization. RESULTS: ASDS induced presynaptic depression at anterior vSUB (avSUB) [->] AHN synapses through a glucocorticoid- and cannabinoid type 1 receptor (CB1R)-dependent mechanism, while posterior vSUB (pvSUB) [->] AHN synapses were unaffected. Infusing a CB1R antagonist into the AHN before ASDS attenuated both the synaptic depression and the social avoidance. Chemogenetic activation of the avSUB [->] AHN pathway during ASDS attenuated social avoidance, whereas its inhibition induced avoidance under subthreshold stress. Optogenetic activation of the avSUB [->] AHN pathway produced an immediate increase in social approach. Anterograde tracing revealed that anterior and posterior vSUB neurons project to largely separate AHN populations. The pvSUB [->] AHN pathway modulates anxiety-like behavior without altering social approach. CONCLUSIONS: These findings reveal specialized roles for vSUB subregions in social and emotional responses, and identify presynaptic gating of the avSUB [->] AHN synapse as a control point for stress-induced social withdrawal.

title: Network Localization of Anxiety as an Early Manifestation of Alzheimer's Disease-related Neurodegeneration
authors: Lee, S.; Ha, J.; Garimella, A. H.; Baratono, S. R.; Burt, G. T.; Karim, H. T.; Andreescu, C.; Sperling, R. A.; Donovan, N. J.; Fox, M. D.; Siddiqi, S. H.
abstract: Objective Anxiety is a prominent neuropsychiatric symptom in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neural circuitry linking anxiety and AD remains uncharacterized. We assessed whether anxiety in preclinical AD is independently associated with AD-related neurodegeneration and localizes to a common anxiety network. Methods In cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults with 3T MRI and amyloid-beta PET (N=1,775), we examined whether an established AD-related atrophy network is associated with anxiety (STAI-6). Then, using Atrophy Network Mapping (ANM), which maps individual cortical atrophy patterns onto a normative functional connectome (N=1000), we derived an anxiety network. We tested its 1) spatial convergence with the AD network and with a causal anxiety network derived from lesion and neuromodulation data, 2) specificity relative to depression, 3) generalizability in samples from independent cohorts with AD and Parkinson's disease (total n=878), and 4) association with longitudinal outcomes. Results In CU older adults, greater AD-network atrophy was associated with higher anxiety, independent of depression, cognition, cortical atrophy, and amyloid burden. Anxiety localized to a network closely resembling the AD network (r=0.74, p=0.04) and the causal anxiety network (r=0.72, p=0.02). This convergence extended across the AD continuum and to the Parkinson's disease cohort and was specific to anxiety relative to depression. Greater anxiety-network atrophy was associated with cognitive decline over 4.6 years. Conclusion Anxiety localizes to a brain circuit resembling the AD-related atrophy network, is consistent across the AD continuum and may extend beyond AD. These findings support anxiety as an independent marker of early AD-related neurodegeneration.

title: PACAP engages distinct signaling programs across cortical neuronal and non-neuronal cell types
authors: Heimbach, S. N.; Collazos Matute, A.; Dolman, B.; Bald, V.; Melzer, S.
abstract: Neuropeptides form modulatory communication channels that tune neuronal circuits and their functions, often through selective targeting of distinct cell populations. Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) is an important neuropeptidergic regulator of fear and stress. However, its receptors are surprisingly ubiquitous across most brain areas and cell types, making the physiological roles and functional mechanisms difficult to predict. Here, we investigate the cell type-specific effects of PACAP in the temporal association cortex (TeA), a brain region implicated in fear learning and memory. Adcyap1r1, encoding the PACAP receptor PAC1, was broadly expressed across the majority of neuronal and non-neuronal cells. Yet, PACAP engaged highly diverse molecular pathways across functionally distinct cell types that were differentially recruited during auditory fear learning and retrieval, providing a framework for how broad receptor expression can yield specific network modulation. Our data underscore the importance of dissecting cellularly resolved peptidergic signaling to understand functional mechanisms of neuropeptides.

title: Specialized and experience-dependent neural dynamics in the medial amygdala and bed nucleus of stria terminalis upon social and sexual olfactory and tactile cues
authors: Huijgens, P. T.; Heijkoop, R.; Snoeren, E. M. S.
abstract: The medial amygdala (MeApd) and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) are central components of the social behavior network. However, their real-time activity during social and sexual interactions, and their respective contributions to processing olfactory and tactile cues, remain unclear. Here, we used simultaneous dual site fiber photometry to record GCaMP6s signals from the MeApd and BNST in freely behaving male rats during social interaction, copulation, sexual exhaustion, and vaginal occlusion tests. Introduction of a conspecific increased activity in both regions, but the response profiles differed by social context and experience. The MeApd responded robustly to male and female conspecifics, with larger responses to males, whereas BNST activity increased reliably upon female introduction only after sexual experience. During olfactory investigation of a male conspecific, MeApd activity differentiated sniffing of anterior and posterior body regions, while BNST activity showed no comparable spatial selectivity. Neither region showed robust event-aligned responses during sniffing of receptive females. Tactile stimulation during copulation elicited strong calcium responses in both regions. Mounts, intromissions, and ejaculations each triggered significant activity, with ejaculation producing the largest responses. MeApd responses differentiated ejaculation from mounting in sexually naive animals, whereas distinctions in BNST responses emerged primarily after sexual experience. Moreover, responses to intromissions and ejaculations persisted during the final ejaculatory series preceding sexual exhaustion, while responses to mounts were eliminated when vaginal penetration was prevented. Together, these findings identify specialized yet parallel activity dynamics within the MeApd-BNST network. MeApd activity preferentially tracks socially relevant olfactory investigation and the intensity of copulatory sensory feedback, whereas BNST recruitment during sexual behavior is more strongly shaped by sexual experience.

title: High-dimensional hippocampus representation facilitates learning of low-dimensional abstract representation and supports generalization
authors: Wang, B.; Johnston, W. J.; Fusi, S.
abstract: Semantic knowledge encompasses facts, concepts, and their relationships. Recent work has proposed that some forms of semantic knowledge could be encoded in low-dimensional neural representations, such as the abstract, disentangled representational geometries observed in many cognitive brain areas. Experimental work has shown that hippocampal (HPC) lesions impair the formation of flexible and generalizable semantic knowledge. However, HPC representations are often high-dimensional and sparse. How can these representations contribute to the formation of low-dimensional abstract representation across these cognitive cortical areas? Here, we reconcile these observations using multiregional neural network models. Modeling HPC as a sparse, decorrelating autoencoder, we show that its high-dimensional representations promote the robust and efficient formation of low-dimensional abstract representations in downstream regions such as prefrontal cortex. This effect is most pronounced when the geometry of sensory inputs is misaligned with the geometry of desired outputs, requiring a more complex input-output transformation. Mathematical analysis shows that hippocampal expansion recoding suppresses misleading low-dimensional input structure and reshapes the loss landscape of downstream networks, allowing abstract semantic geometry to emerge reliably. The resulting abstract representations provide an inductive bias for sample-efficient learning of novel semantic-to-action mappings. Finally, we show that consolidating hippocampus-dependent representations into a hippocampus-independent pathway improves out-of-distribution generalization based on input structure. Together, these results suggest a circuit mechanism by which high-dimensional hippocampal representations can support, rather than oppose, the emergence of low-dimensional abstract representations.

title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
authors: Feng, G.; Chen, J.; Iraji, A.; Sendi, M. S. E.; Fu, Z.; Calhoun, V. D.
abstract: Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6-80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

title: PhaseICA: Resolving Individual-Specific Macroscale Brain Propagations
authors: Ma, L.; Li, Q.; Adali, T.; Iraji, A.; Fu, Z.; Calhoun, V.
abstract: Understanding complex dynamics from spatiotemporal signals requires robust tools capable of decoding reoccurring patterns. Traditional ICA methods often overlook the spatially non-stationarity nature of brain activity across both the frequency and spatial domains. We propose a novel data-driven approach, named PhaseICA, designed to extract reoccurring spatiotemporal patterns, referred to as brain waves. Unlike conventional ICA methods that focus solely on amplitude, PhaseICA incorporates phase information directly into the component estimation, preserving the nonstationary property that real-valued ICA methods typically discard. The method performs spatial independence optimization in the complex domain by minimizing a complex entropy bound over the eigenvectors of Hilbert-transformed signals. The proposed method captures spatial propagation across brain regions with interpretable and compact representations, offering a promising foundation for decoding brain dynamic systems and revealing the temporal relationship of regions.

title: EcoHIV Treated Primary Microglia Exhibit a Highly Specialized and Sex-Dependent Transcriptional State
authors: Veenstra, B. J.; Nelson, K.; Elder, T. R.; Turner, J. R.; McLaurin, K. A.
abstract: The pathogenesis of HIV-1-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) is partly driven by microglial dysregulation. Indeed, HIV-1-induced microglial dyshomeostasis is characterized by a sustained pro-inflammatory state and exacerbated microglia proliferation. Herein, in vitro studies were conducted in primary microglia to elucidate the transcriptomic alterations underlying EcoHIV induced microglia hyperproliferation. Consistent with, and expanding upon, prior studies, treatment with EcoHIV exacerbated microglia proliferation evidenced by the upregulation of Pcna and Mki67. With regards to microglial receptors and adapter proteins, the transcriptomic expression of Trem2 and Dap12 was suppressed and increased, respectively, in microglia treated with EcoHIV. Crucially, dysregulation of the Trem2/Dap12 signaling complex explained 51.4% of the variance in microglial proliferation in EcoHIV treated microglia. A preliminary investigation of the Trem2-mediated microglial survival and immunoregulation pathway affords additional support for a unique EcoHIV-induced transcriptomic profile. Specifically, independent of biological sex, EcoHIV treatment upregulated Syk and downregulated Ctnnb1 mRNA expression. Notably, biological sex regulates precisely how EcoHIV treated microglia respond to the suppression of Trem2 and compensatory hyperproliferative state. Collectively, primary microglia treated with EcoHIV exhibit a highly specialized and sex-dependent transcriptional state. Enhancing our understanding of how HIV-1 alters microglial homeostasis is crucial for the identification of novel therapeutic targets for HAND.

title: A clinically identified Kirrel3 variant disrupts trans-synaptic circuit assembly
authors: Shennib, O.; Johnson, A.; Raines, O.; Williams, M. E.
abstract: Trans-synaptic adhesion molecules guide selective connections between neurons to establish circuit specificity. Yet, there are gaps in the understanding of how many synaptic adhesion molecules function in vivo and if clinically identified variants perturb their function. Using cell-type-specific deletion in the mouse hippocampus, we show that Kirrel3 is required in both pre-synaptic DG neurons and post-synaptic GABA neurons to form DG-to-GABA excitatory synapses that drive a feed-forward inhibitory connection to CA3. These data provide in vivo, genetic evidence for a homophilic trans-synaptic Kirrel3 interaction driving synapse formation. Moderately increasing or decreasing wildtype Kirrel3 expression did not detectably alter synapse formation or CA3 neuron activity. In contrast, expression of a Kirrel3 missense variant identified in an individual with autism dominantly disrupts synapse formation and CA3 activity in vivo, providing a mechanism by which a single missense allele could disrupt circuit assembly and contribute to disease.

title: The marginal brain
authors: Lokwani-Di Matteo, F.; Sacco, P. L.
abstract: Goal-directed cognition raises brain energy use only a few percent above resting use, a figure often read as evidence that cognition is metabolically cheap. Models of endogenous precision derive the precision of neural representations from a cost on encoding activity whose unit price is a free parameter. Embedding endogenous precision in a regulated, shared energy budget makes this cost the shadow price of energy at the margin of the budget. Neither the task share of the budget nor the net whole-brain increment identifies this price; when tasks face a common price ratio and coding technology is stable, imprecision changes by the exact fourth root of that ratio, so that the cost of information rescales while its shape is preserved; and the co-movement of imprecision and stimulus-linked task energy separates price changes from changes in coding technology. In 12,960 published estimation trials, response variance at matched numerosities rises with prior width in line with the ratios that the calibrated model predicts out of sample, and simulations indicate that a doubled price is detectable with existing paradigms when state-dependent lapses are modeled.

title: FTO does not function as an m6A eraser in AML: a reassessment using direct RNA nanopore sequencing
authors: Nicholson, L. S.; Guimaraes-Teixeira, C.; Liu, J. F.; Chien, R.; Xu, J.; Poh, H. X.; Pan, Y.-X.; Jaffrey, S. R.
abstract: A central concept in epitranscriptomics is that the RNA demethylase FTO acts as a site-selective eraser of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) in specific mRNAs. This is most well-established in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where demethylation of MYC is thought to promote leukemogenesis. Using nanopore direct RNA sequencing to quantify m6A transcriptome-wide, we find that m6A stoichiometry, including at MYC-specific sites, remains unaffected by FTO knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition in AML. Conversely, levels of N6-2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) are markedly increased in snRNAs, indicating that m6Am, not m6A, is the major substrate of FTO in AML. We extend these results outside the AML context in FTO knockout brain and HEK293T cells, detecting no selective increases in mRNA m6A but widespread increases in snRNA m6Am levels following FTO depletion. These findings suggest that FTO has minimal ability to erase m6A in mRNA. Instead, the reported biological effects of FTO are likely mediated by demethylation of m6Am.

title: A unique intestinal epithelial cell that expresses canonical lymphoid genes
authors: Bhattacharya, S.; Badarinath, K.; Tie, G.; Singh, P. N. P.; Eskiocak, O.; He, R.; Bao, B.; Lee, S.-H.; Snapper, S. B.; Huang, K.; Goldenring, J. R.; Beyaz, S.; Shivdasani, R. A.
abstract: Enterocytes and intestinal secretory cells harbor innate immunity. However, certain transcriptional programs -even beyond rearranged T- and B-cell receptor genes- are considered the exclusive purview of adaptive immune cells, including abundant and diverse intestinal intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IELs). Here, we identify and characterize columnar intestinal secretory cells that co-express classic epithelial and lymphoid genes, including Ptprc, Cd3e, Cd8a, and Gzma/b but not T- or B-cell receptors. These previously unrecognized epithelium-derived lymphoid-like cells (EDLCs) differ from any known resident cell type, including IELs or tuft cells. Rare in healthy mouse and human intestines, their numbers increase upon IL-25 stimulation or IL-10 receptor deficiency in vivo and upon IL-13 stimulation in vitro. EDLC chromatin is uniquely accessible at thousands of cis-elements, including lymphoid and epithelial loci. These findings reveal a transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct intestinal epithelial derivative that expresses prominent lymphoid character.
